title: Eric Schmidt Says AI Could Let Large Companies Cut 20% of Staff
excerpt: The former Google chief executive told the In Good Company podcast that a 10,000-person company may have 'a couple of thousand people who you don't need' once AI agents take over coordination work.
body:
• Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt said AI could let large companies operate with about 20% fewer staff — roughly 2,000 roles in a 10,000-person company.
  • The roles at risk, in his account, are the 'glue people': planning, coordination and moving information between teams. Sales, product building, leadership and work with regulators remain human jobs.
  • Schmidt, speaking to Norges Bank's Nicolai Tangen, also said Chinese open-weight AI models trail the US frontier by only about six months, and put true machine discovery — his AGI boundary — five to ten years away.
  • For readers in large-company coordination roles: Schmidt's advice to employers was to transition affected staff 'legally and humanely'; he offered no timeline for when the cuts arrive.

Eric Schmidt ran Google for a decade, and he describes the job plainly: meetings, 12 hours a day, five days a week, plus weekends — about 63 hours of coordination. His argument now is that AI platforms can eliminate much of that 'coordination tax', and with it a fifth of the workforce of a large company.

Speaking on the In Good Company podcast with Nicolai Tangen, chief executive of Norges Bank Investment Management, Schmidt estimated that a 10,000-person company has, in his words, "a couple of thousand people who you don't need" — and that leaders must find a legal, humane way to transition them out.

"Let's say you're running a 10,000-person company, my guess is you've got a couple of thousand people who you don't need. And you better figure out a way to legally and humanely transition them, retire them out, or what have you."

— Eric Schmidt, former CEO, Google

Which jobs, in his telling

Schmidt cited a friend whose fast-growing company cut 20% of its staff. The cuts fell on the 'glue people' — those planning projects and moving numbers around — while salespeople, people who talk to regulators, and product builders stayed in demand. He said the friend received death threats over the layoffs. As coverage of the interview noted, Schmidt expects that pattern to become more common as AI agents take over gathering updates, passing them upward and keeping teams aligned.

He was blunt about adoption: he holds a strong view that almost none of the companies listening will actually make the cultural changes required, even though agentic AI is, in his phrase, a powerful flattening of the organisation.

The wider AI picture

Schmidt rejected the idea that AI is a bubble, pointing to Anthropic's revenue growth — more than twice as fast as Google's at its peak, in his telling. His sharper warning was geopolitical: Chinese open-weight models trail the US frontier by only about six months, and because they are free, much of the world may end up running them. He put true machine discovery, his definition of the AGI boundary, five to ten years away, and said AI treaties are likely to arrive only after an accident.

Schmidt's numbers are a prediction, not a plan announced by any employer. But they land in a year when large technology firms have repeatedly cut coordination and management layers while reporting record AI-driven revenue — which is why a former CEO's estimate, delivered on a sovereign wealth fund's podcast, is being read as a planning assumption rather than a provocation.
